item.question: A transparent circle is placed on the angle of the first crane with its centre at the vertex; A and B are marked where the arms cross the circle. The circle is then placed on the second crane's angle with the vertex at the centre and one arm through OA. Can you now tell which angle is bigger?
steps: Match one arm of each angle with OA.
Compare the other end points on the circle (B and Y).
A farther end point means a bigger angle.
item.answer: Compare where the second arm meets the circle, at Y, with the point B. If Y is beyond B the second angle is bigger, if Y falls on B they are equal, and if Y falls short of B it is smaller. Here Y is very close to B, so the two angles are nearly equal.

If the slit angle is greater than the arms' angle, the arms will not go through.
If the slit angle is less than the arms' angle, the arms will not go through.
If equal, the arms go through.
item.answer: Only the arm whose angle is equal to the slit's angle passes through; place each over the slit to find it. Passing through depends only on the angle, not on the arms' lengths (as long as they are shorter than the slit).
item.text:
Worked example: Collect a number of rotating arms with different angles (do not rotate any of them). Take a cardboard and make an angle-shaped slit by tracing and cutting out the shape of one of the rotating arms. Now shuffle and mix up all the rotating arms. Can you identify which of the rotating arms will pass through the slit?
1. Place an arm over the slit.
2. If the slit angle is greater than the arms' angle, the arms will not go through.
3. If the slit angle is less than the arms' angle, the arms will not go through.
4. If equal, the arms go through.
Answer: Only the arm whose angle is equal to the slit's angle passes through; place each over the slit to find it. Passing through depends only on the angle, not on the arms' lengths (as long as they are shorter than the slit).

concept_name: Cutting the arms does not shrink the angle

item.question: Challenge: Reduce this angle. (A girl snips the ends of the arms of a V-shaped rotating arm with scissors: 'Angle reduced.' The boy says 'The angle is still the same!')
steps: Cutting shortens the arms but the opening stays the same.
To reduce the angle, rotate one arm closer to the other.
item.answer: Cutting the arms shorter does not change the angle; the size of an angle depends only on the amount of turn between the arms, not on their length. To reduce the angle, bring the arms closer together (turn one arm).

concept_name: Folding a straight angle in half

item.question: Justify why the two angles are equal. Is there a way to superimpose and check? Can this superimposition be done by folding?
steps: Fold along crease OC.
OA and OB coincide, so ∠AOC fits on ∠COB.
So they are equal.
item.answer: Because OB was folded onto OA, the two arms overlap exactly, so the two angles fit exactly on each other and are equal. Yes, folding itself is the superimposition: fold along the crease and the two angles coincide.
